title: WHO Says Childhood Obesity Needs More Than Medicine: A Family-First Plan
excerpt: WHO's first global childhood obesity guidelines bar drugs and surgery for under-10s and put diet, activity, sleep and caregiver support first for all ages.
body:
• The World Health Organization released its first global guidelines on childhood obesity on October 7, putting structured eating, activity and behaviour support ahead of medicines.
  • WHO does not recommend weight-loss drugs, surgery or devices for children aged 0 to 9; for ages 10 to 19, medicines may be considered only after a supervised lifestyle programme has not worked.
  • About 400 million people aged 5 to 19 were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity; prevalence in that group rose from 2% in 1990 to 8% in 2024, an increase of 6 percentage points.
  • For families: aim for an average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity for ages 5 to 17, protect sleep, and do not start weight-loss medicines or restrictive diets without a clinician.

The World Health Organization has told families and doctors to treat childhood obesity first with food, movement, sleep and behaviour support, not with a prescription. In its first global guidelines for children and adolescents, released on October 7, the agency said medicines and surgery have a narrow place, and no place at all for younger children.

The guidance, reported by Reuters and detailed for Indian readers by the Times of India, arrives as demand grows for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. WHO said there is still insufficient evidence on those drugs in young people and that guidance may change as trials report.

What WHO actually recommends

For children aged 0 to 9, WHO does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery or weight-loss devices. Instead it strongly recommends structured dietary, physical activity and behaviour-change programmes, delivered individually or combined, with caregivers involved. Digital support is an option only under parental supervision, according to coverage by Medical Xpress / AFP.

For adolescents aged 10 to 19, approved medicines may be considered only when a supervised multimodal programme has not achieved the desired result. Surgery may be considered under strict conditions for physically and mentally mature adolescents with severe obesity, after about six months of unsuccessful treatment and where complications such as type 2 diabetes or hypertension are present.

"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery"

— Luz María De Regil, WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, via Reuters

The numbers in absolute terms

WHO put the global total at about 400 million children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 who were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity. That is 170 million individual children, not a rate. Prevalence rose from 2% in 1990 to 8% in 2024. In absolute terms that is a rise of 6 percentage points, even though it is often described as a fourfold increase.

India shows the same direction in younger children. Figures cited from the National Family Health Survey put overweight and obesity among children under five at 1.5% in NFHS-3 in 2005-06 and 3.4% in NFHS-5 in 2019-21, a rise of 1.9 percentage points. Adolescent overweight and obesity also rose between those surveys.

What this means for Indian families

Doctors quoted in the Indian coverage stressed small, shared changes rather than singling out a child. Home-cooked meals built around dal, roti, vegetables, seasonal fruit, curd, pulses and whole grains can remain the base; the change is in preparation, portions and how often sugary drinks and packaged snacks appear. Forcing a child to finish a plate or imposing a drastic diet was specifically discouraged.

Two household habits matter as much as the menu. First, stop using sweets routinely as a reward; time together, play or reading can mark an achievement without training a food loop. Second, make movement ordinary: walking, cycling, dance, active games or sport that fits the child's age and interests, spread across the week to reach the 60-minute daily average WHO cites for ages 5 to 17.

Screen time and sleep are part of the same routine. Eating together without phones, keeping a consistent bedtime and leaving gaps between schoolwork, tuition and recreational screens were presented as practical starting points, in India and in diaspora homes where commutes and tutoring compress the evening in the same way.

Where medicines still fit

WHO is not ruling out treatment. Some GLP-1 medicines are already approved for certain adolescents aged 12 and older in the United States and the European Union. The new guidance sets a sequence: structured support first, specialist assessment next, and medicines or surgery only for the older, more severe cases that meet the conditions. Parents should not give a child weight-loss medicine, or borrow an adult prescription, without paediatric guidance.

Schools and communities carry part of the load too, through active breaks, sports and safe places to play.
